Members of the Iron County militia of the Nauvoo Legion, with some Southern Paiute men
One man, John D. Lee, tried twice, convicted and executed in 1877
17 young children, spared by the killers; the sources give their ages as under seven (HistoryNet) or six and younger (Fox News, citing the 2007 coverage)
About 140 men, women and children according to Will Bagley in HistoryNet; the Utah Communication History Encyclopedia, citing a different passage of Bagley's book, gives 65 members
Four days according to National Geographic and American History Central; five days according to HistoryNet and the Utah State Archives
Isaac C. Haight and John D. Lee; Colonel William Dame commanded the district militia

content.p: In the second week of September 1857, a wagon train of emigrants from Arkansas, bound for California, was besieged in a high valley in southern Utah Territory. On Friday 11 September the attackers, local Mormon militiamen, persuaded the emigrants to give up their weapons in return for an escort to safety. Then they killed about 120 of them. Only 17 small children were spared. The historian Will Bagley, writing in Wild West magazine, wrote that those most guilty of the crime explained it with "denials, lies and alibis that twisted and turned as the evidence inevitably came out".

For nearly two decades no one was prosecuted, and the official Mormon account blamed local Paiute people alone. Only one man, John D. Lee, was ever convicted. He was executed at the massacre site in March 1877. In 2007 a senior leader of The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints expressed "profound regret" for the killings and placed the responsibility on local church leaders. Historians still argue about how far the order went up the chain of command.

Mormon settlers had reached Utah in 1847 after being driven from New York, Missouri and Illinois, and their founder Joseph Smith had been killed by a mob in Illinois in 1844, National Geographic recounts. Congress refused them a state of their own and made Utah a territory instead, with Brigham Young as its first governor. During the 1850s, relations with federal appointees in the territory soured. American History Central says that one of them, Judge W. W. Drummond, wrote to the new president, James Buchanan, complaining that Young was defying orders from Washington.

In 1857 Buchanan removed Young as governor and sent troops to install a replacement. The Juanita Brooks lecture notes that the army's approach was announced to the Mormons only by rumour; the frontiersman Orrin Porter Rockwell brought confirmation on 24 July. American History Central puts the expedition at roughly 1,500 troops, while the lecture speaks of 2,500. Young declared martial law on 5 August, the Utah Communication History Encyclopedia records. Settlers were told to store food, and LDS Living says they were told not to sell grain or ammunition to passing emigrants.

The farther from Salt Lake City, the greater the war fever, the lecture says, quoting one Mormon who described Cedar City as at "fever heat". It records that Apostle George A. Smith toured the southern settlements in late August. Asked whether he would wait for instructions before attacking any invaders, Major Isaac Haight of the Iron County militia replied that "there would be no time to wait for instructions".

The emigrants were from Arkansas, led by veteran plainsmen including Alexander Fancher and John Baker. Bagley describes a dozen prosperous families with a number of wagons, several hundred cattle and blooded horses for sale in California. His figure for the whole company is about 140 people, women and children outnumbering able-bodied men two to one. The Utah Communication History Encyclopedia, quoting a different page of Bagley's book Blood of the Prophets, gives 65 members; the sources do not reconcile the numbers.

They found Mormon settlers unwilling to trade. National Geographic says the mostly Methodist travellers quarrelled with locals over supplies, and that clashes around Cedar City set Fancher against militia leaders such as John D. Lee and Haight. LDS Living, a church-aligned outlet, says that stories of the emigrants poisoning a spring and an ox carcass have been proven false, and that the emigrants appear to have made only idle threats, which their captains rebuked. Another motive appears in a quotation the Utah Communication History Encyclopedia takes from Bagley's book, which has Lee saying the company had men "supposed to have helped kill the Prophets in the Carthage jail", so that killing them would be "avenging the blood of the prophets". The same essay lists the motives for the attack as speculation.

LDS Living says Haight asked the district militia commander, Colonel William Dame of Parowan, for permission to punish the emigrants, and that Dame at first refused: "Words are but wind". The Juanita Brooks lecture records a night council of militia officers at Parowan, after which Dame decided the party should be allowed to leave in peace, though an unsubstantiated account says he and Haight later reversed that. According to LDS Living, Haight and Lee then planned to persuade Southern Paiutes to attack the emigrants and so shift the blame.

The assault began at dawn on Monday 7 September, Bagley writes. A volley of gunfire and arrows killed or wounded about a quarter of the adult men, but the survivors drove the first attack back, drew their wagons into a circle and dug a pit to shelter the women and children. Cut off from water, they held out under fire. National Geographic and American History Central call this a four-day siege; Bagley and the Utah State Archives say five. HistoryNet's introduction to the article adds that both sides were growing desperate: the emigrants were short of food and water, and the militia feared being recognised as something other than Native Americans, which would complicate the war.

The Brooks lecture says that Lee, at one point close to the emigrant camp, was seen by emigrants who had raised a white flag in the middle of their corral. LDS Living says that, because the emigrants now knew they had been attacked by settlers and not only by Paiutes, Dame gave Haight and Lee permission to act.

On Friday 11 September a Mormon emissary under a white flag entered the wagon fort, followed by Lee, whom Bagley calls the local Indian agent. Bagley says Lee told the emigrants he had come to rescue them from the Indians, and that if they laid down their arms the militia would escort them to safety. The emigrants had few options and surrendered.

Bagley's account has the wounded and youngest children driven out first in two wagons, women and older children walking behind and the men last, each beside an armed guard. After more than a mile the senior officer gave an order, perhaps "Halt!" but by most accounts "Do your duty!". Each guard shot the man beside him. Men dressed or painted as Native Americans, "a few of whom may have been actual Indians", killed the women and children, while Lee directed the killing of the wounded. Bagley says it was over within five minutes. Nancy Cates, a survivor, recalled in 1875, quoted by National Geographic, that some of the young women begged not to be killed but the attackers "had no mercy".

Seventeen children were spared. Bagley says the killers judged them too young to be credible witnesses and counted them as "innocent blood" under Mormon doctrine. LDS Living quotes Turley as saying that Nephi Johnson later maintained that the militiamen, not the Paiutes, did most of the killing. Forest Cuch, then head of the Utah Division of Indian Affairs, argued in 2007 that only a few Paiutes took part and that the church should say there were 60 militia and two Paiutes.

The Utah State Archives says that the Mormon officials' official story was that Paiutes alone had done it. Bagley says the killers took the company's property and cash, and that much of it apparently went to Brigham Young, a claim Bagley makes in his own voice. He adds that no compensation was ever offered to the survivors. The bodies were buried hastily and so shallowly that they were partly exposed.

The Brooks lecture dates the first wave of investigation to 1859: Indian agent Jacob Forney, army major James Carleton and Judge John Cradlebaugh, each reporting to a different department. Bagley says Forney went south for the surviving children, whose statements identified Lee as one of the killers; his party headed north with 16 of them. Bagley also says that Jacob Hamblin, the Indian missionary, told Brigham Young "everything" about the murders in June 1858, including that white men were involved, and that Young told him not to speak of it. The lecture adds that the Civil War brought the Forney-Carleton-Cradlebaugh era of investigation to a close.

After a federal judge began investigating, the Utah State Archives says, Lee went into hiding. The Archives also records that he was excommunicated in 1870 and that Young instructed him to keep out of sight in northern Arizona.
content.h2: Two trials of John D. Lee
content.p: In 1871 federal officials obtained a sworn statement from Philip Klingensmith, a former Cedar City bishop who had left the church, according to the Brooks lecture. The Poland Act of 1874 loosened Mormon control of the territorial courts, the Archives explains, and Lee was arrested and tried at Beaver.

The first trial began in July 1875. The Archives says the prosecution tried to lay most of the blame on the church leadership, Brigham Young foremost among them. The jury of eight Mormons, one former Mormon and three non-Mormons hung, and everyone but the three non-Mormons voted to acquit. At the second trial the prosecution put the blame squarely on Lee as the driving force. Lee asked that no defence be made, believing he was being made a scapegoat, and an all-Mormon jury found him guilty of first-degree murder. He was sentenced to death by firing squad. The Archives has digitised the case file.

Lee was shot at Mountain Meadows. The Archives gives the date as 28 March 1877, and his body was taken to Panguitch for burial. The Brooks lecture and a student essay on the Utah Communication History Encyclopedia both give 23 March; the essay's page carries the Salt Lake Tribune's report of 24 March 1877. Bagley says Lee was regarded as a scapegoat by his descendants and by historians alike.

Isaac Haight, John Higbee and William Stewart were never arrested, according to the Brooks lecture. In 1879 Judge Jacob Boreman suggested to the attorney general a private reward of $500 for each, but money for further prosecutions never came. Haight, the lecture says, went to Chihuahua in Mexico and died a fugitive. Dame was held in custody, released on bail in May 1876, and in September 1876 the U.S. attorney entered a nolle prosequi.

Bagley describes two memorials. Descendants and the state of Utah paid for a granite monument on Dan's Hill overlooking the killing ground in 1990. The church raised a second in 1999 above the victims' grave; Bagley says a backhoe accidentally uncovered their remains while it was being built in haste. Patty Norris, president of the Mountain Meadows Massacre Descendants, said in 2007 that Gordon B. Hinckley had ruled out an apology when he presided at the 1999 ceremony.

On 11 September 2007, the 150th anniversary, Elder Henry B. Eyring of the Quorum of the Twelve addressed several hundred people at the site. He said, "We express profound regret for the massacre carried out in this valley 150 years ago today, and for the undue and untold suffering experienced by the victims then and by their relatives to the present time." He cited church historians who put responsibility on local leaders in Cedar City and those acting under them, and said Young had tried to send word protecting the wagon train, but that the message did not arrive in time. He also expressed regret to the Paiutes, who he said had "unjustly borne for too long the principal blame".

The church spokesman Mark Tuttle told the Associated Press that the church did not use the word "apology", and that the statement was "profound regret". Norris called it as close to an apology as descendants had come and "the first time the church admitted" that church people were involved. Bagley wrote that for 150 years leaders and official historians of the church worked to justify or explain away the crime. National Geographic notes that historians still ask whether Mormon leaders condoned or planned it, and says that given the lack of evidence those questions may never be answered.
